problem_plain: When many chips work together to train or run an AI model, they must constantly share data — passing partial results, keeping copies of shared values in sync, and coordinating who does what next. The wires and switches that carry this traffic (the interconnect) have a fixed, physically limited capacity. As models and clusters grow, the volume of data that must move between chips grows faster than the capacity of those wires, turning the network into the primary bottleneck. The result is that expensive chips sit idle, waiting for data to arrive rather than doing arithmetic.
why_plain: Physics sets hard limits: more wires cost more area and power, and signals degrade over distance. You cannot simply add bandwidth the way you can add compute cores. Meanwhile, AI models keep growing, meaning more devices must share more data at once — the demand outpaces what physics cheaply allows.
approach_plain: Papers in this theme attack the bottleneck from three angles: reduce how much data needs to move (compression, smarter partitioning, eliminating redundant transfers), move the data more efficiently (better routing, topology-matched algorithms, overlapping transfers with computation), and rethink the hardware fabric itself (new topologies, smarter switches that process data in-flight, and purpose-built physical layers). The common thread is that saving one byte of network traffic or one millisecond of idle time compounds across thousands of chips and billions of training steps.

groups.heading: Hiding communication behind computation — overlap and scheduling
groups.explain: When a chip finishes its local arithmetic, it must send results to other chips before everyone can move to the next step. If the chip simply waits, that waiting time is pure waste. The trick is to start sending early — splitting large messages into smaller pieces, sending the first piece while computing the second, so the network and the arithmetic units stay busy at the same time. This requires a compiler or runtime that knows exactly when each piece of data will be ready and can pre-schedule its delivery.

papers.name: Concerto
papers.gloss: Compiler that automatically splits blocking collective messages (where all chips must wait for each other) into pieces and schedules them to overlap with ongoing computation, working across any combination of parallelism strategies; reportedly matches or beats Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed.

papers.name: TileLink
papers.gloss: Programming system that expresses compute and inter-GPU data transfer at the tile (small matrix block) level, then compiles both into a single GPU kernel; achieves 1.17–20.76x speedup over non-overlapping baselines with roughly one-tenth the hand-written code.

papers.name: MeshSlice
papers.gloss: 2D tensor-parallelism algorithm for TPU clusters that slices collective reductions into many small partial operations interleaved with matrix multiply, hiding most communication latency; 12–23% faster than prior art on 256 TPUs.

papers.name: Chimera
papers.gloss: Analyzes how combining multiple parallelism strategies (splitting model, pipeline, data) creates redundant back-to-back collective messages, then fuses them into one; delivers 1.32–1.58x faster forward passes on AI chips called NPUs (dedicated neural-network processors).

groups.heading: Smarter collective operations — algorithms matched to physical wiring
groups.explain: A collective operation is when every chip in a group must contribute to — and receive — a shared result, such as adding up gradient values from all workers. The naive approach treats the network as a black box and uses generic ring or tree patterns that often collide on the same wires. A better approach designs the communication pattern to match the actual topology of wires, so data flows with the grain of the network rather than against it, using every link at full capacity.

papers.name: TidalMesh
papers.gloss: AllReduce (sum-across-all-chips) algorithm designed natively for 2D grid (mesh) networks; pushes data in wave patterns that align with the grid, achieving up to 24% better AllReduce performance on a 64-node 8x8 grid versus adapted ring/tree methods.

papers.name: Vocabulary Parallelism
papers.gloss: Spreads the word-embedding layer (the lookup table that maps text tokens to numbers) evenly across all pipeline stages, reducing synchronization barriers from 3 to 1 per pass; improves pipeline-parallel LLM training throughput by 5–51%.

papers.name: vNPU
papers.gloss: Virtualizes inter-core connected AI chips (like Graphcore IPU) by making routing, memory addressing, and topology all aware of the physical wiring layout; multiple workloads share one device up to 1.92x faster than naive partitioning.

papers.name: PIMnet
papers.gloss: Builds a dedicated multi-tier network between processing-in-memory units (compute logic embedded inside DRAM chips) so they can collectively sum results without routing through the host CPU; up to 85x faster on collective operations, 11.8x on real applications.

groups.heading: Reducing how much data moves — compression, sparsity, and redundancy elimination
groups.explain: The simplest way to relieve a congested road is to put fewer cars on it. For chip networks this means sending only the data that is truly needed: compressing gradient values (the updates each chip sends after processing a batch), skipping values that are near zero, deduplicating requests that ask for the same data, and reorganizing which chip stores which data so fewer cross-chip transfers are needed in the first place.

papers.name: Radius
papers.gloss: Observes that the most important gradient indices (the positions of the largest updates) stay stable after the first 15–20% of training; reuses those indices to send only the gradient values via a cheap all-reduce instead of an expensive all-gather, cutting communication by up to 90% and speeding training 19% on 128 GPUs.

papers.name: Frugal
papers.gloss: Makes recommendation-model training practical on cheap GPUs lacking fast inter-GPU links by rearranging which embedding rows (rows of a lookup table for users/items) live on which GPU to minimize cross-GPU traffic, then compressing gradients and overlapping transfers; targets commodity clusters with no direct GPU-to-GPU memory access.

papers.name: TRACI
papers.gloss: Adds hardware inside network switches to detect when multiple GPUs request the same sparse embedding row (row of a user/item lookup table) and aggregates or deduplicates those requests on the fly, before data reaches the GPUs; targets recommendation models where access patterns are input-dependent and unpredictable.

papers.name: DiTile-DGNN
papers.gloss: Accelerator for dynamic graph neural networks (networks whose edges change over time) that analytically finds which data is shared across time steps and avoids recomputing or resending it; cuts execution time 23–56% and energy 71–84% versus prior accelerators.

papers.name: Mithril
papers.gloss: Assigns consecutive neural-network layers to different GPUs instead of splitting the graph across GPUs; each GPU processes the full graph for its layers, reducing per-epoch cross-GPU communication by a factor equal to the number of layers — up to 22.9x less traffic and 7.16x faster on commodity Ethernet.

groups.heading: Network topology and routing — physical wiring that scales
groups.explain: How chips are wired together fundamentally determines worst-case bandwidth and latency. A standard 2D grid of routers is cheap and regular but takes many hops to send data across; a fully connected design is fast but too expensive at scale. Researchers explore new wiring patterns that add a few long-range shortcuts or reorganize the hierarchy of connections to get most of the speed benefit at a fraction of the cost, and pair them with routing rules that exploit the new structure.

papers.name: Zettafly
papers.gloss: Two-layer network topology designed for the next generation of supercomputers: the bottom layer creates small, fully non-blocking groups (where any chip can talk to any other at full speed) and the top layer connects groups through a small number of global routers, keeping diameter low and cost manageable.

papers.name: Ruche Networks
papers.gloss: Augments a standard 2D grid network with uniform long-range bypass links that let non-neighboring routers communicate in fewer hops; RTL-level evaluation shows better power and area efficiency per unit of throughput versus standard mesh and torus networks.

papers.name: EIGEN
papers.gloss: Builds a two-layer network on the active interposer (the silicon bridge connecting multiple chips in a package): one layer uses a programmable switch for static path optimization, the other uses dynamic routing guided by a reinforcement-learning agent; reduces inter-chiplet latency up to 67% and hops up to 54%.

papers.name: FRED
papers.gloss: Places tiny reconfigurable switches across a wafer connecting hundreds of accelerator chiplets; switches can perform partial reductions in-flight (summing values as they pass through) and route different parallelism dimensions over non-overlapping paths; 1.34–1.87x end-to-end training speedup over a 2D mesh wafer baseline.

papers.name: NetCrafter
papers.gloss: Traffic-shaping layer at the boundary between fast intra-group links and slower inter-group links in multi-GPU systems; packs partially-filled data packets together, drops unnecessary prefetch packets, and prioritizes time-critical packets to reduce effective latency.

papers.name: NearFetch
papers.gloss: When a multi-chip GPU module requests data from a remote memory partition, checks whether an intermediate chip along the route already holds that data and forwards it from there instead; cuts average inter-module bandwidth-per-access by 43% and improves performance 52% on data-sharing workloads.

papers.name: Push Multicast
papers.gloss: Makes the shared last-level cache in a many-core processor proactively push data to predicted future requesters the moment it serves any requester, amortizing the per-core network cost; saves 33–43% average network bandwidth in 16- to 64-core chips.

groups.heading: New hardware abstractions — rethinking what the network layer does
groups.explain: Traditional networks just move bytes from point A to point B. Several papers propose making the network itself do useful work: executing atomic read-modify-write operations at the holder of the data rather than bouncing cache lines back and forth, scheduling memory access circuits at the physical signaling layer to cut latency, and bypassing the host CPU from the critical path of network packet handling altogether.

papers.name: EDM
papers.gloss: Implements the remote-memory protocol inside the physical signaling layer of Ethernet (below the MAC, the standard packet-framing logic), eliminating that layer's overhead; achieves roughly 300 nanosecond remote memory access latency — an order of magnitude lower than standard RDMA over Ethernet.

papers.name: Delegato
papers.gloss: Instead of fetching a cache line across chiplet boundaries to perform an atomic add or swap, forwards the operation itself to the chip that already holds the data (a Delegated AMO — read-modify-write done in place); a one-bit reuse signal from private caches guides the directory's routing policy; 1.13x faster than state-of-the-art atomic predictors.

papers.name: AccDirect
papers.gloss: Uses PCIe peer-to-peer direct memory access to connect the network card directly to the CPU's on-chip load-balancing hardware (Intel DLB), removing the host CPU from the critical path of distributing incoming network work; cuts system-wide CPU power by 10% while raising throughput 14–50%.

papers.name: Plaid
papers.gloss: Reconfigurable compute chip (CGRA — a grid of programmable logic cells) where every set of three arithmetic units shares one small local router instead of each unit having its own full crossbar; saves 43–46% power and area versus standard designs while matching their performance.

groups.heading: Parallelism strategies that reshape communication patterns
groups.explain: How you divide a model across chips determines not just how much computation each chip does, but which chips must talk to which, how often, and how much data they exchange. Choosing the right division — or inventing a new kind of division — can eliminate entire categories of communication without changing the model or the hardware.

papers.name: GraphPipe
papers.gloss: Treats a neural network's computation as a branching graph (DAG) rather than a linear sequence and pipelines the branches across device groups concurrently; enables parallelism opportunities that sequential pipeline schemes miss, improving throughput over linear pipeline baselines.

papers.name: Vela
papers.gloss: Runs 50-billion-parameter LLM training on standard cloud virtual machines using commodity Ethernet-based RDMA (rather than expensive InfiniBand) with GPU-direct memory access bypassing the CPU; achieves roughly 80% of ideal throughput at 1,500-GPU scale, documented over 2.5 years of production operation.

papers.name: C4
papers.gloss: Uses the periodic, predictable structure of distributed training's collective synchronization steps as a fault-detection signal — anomalies in the pattern reveal broken hardware immediately; also pre-plans traffic routes to eliminate collisions; cuts error-induced overhead 30% and communication cost 15%.

papers.name: Titan
papers.gloss: Automated design-space exploration framework for wafer-scale data-center chips that jointly optimizes how computation is partitioned and how die-to-die interconnects are configured, pruning infeasible designs early via physical and reliability constraints.

groups.heading: Tools for designing and simulating interconnects
groups.explain: Before you can build a better network, you need to measure the current one accurately and simulate proposed alternatives without spending months on hardware. These papers provide the measurement and simulation infrastructure that makes the rest of the research possible.

papers.name: LEGOSim
papers.gloss: Parallel simulation framework that wraps different chip simulators (CPU, GPU, compute-in-memory) as independent parallel processes synchronized only when they actually exchange messages, not every clock cycle; cuts synchronization overhead up to 99.9% and simulates heterogeneous multi-chiplet systems with under 4% error versus real hardware.

connect: Every paper in this theme is, at root, an answer to the same physical fact: arithmetic inside a chip is cheap and fast, but moving a result to another chip is expensive and slow. Whether researchers are compressing gradients, redesigning routing algorithms, pushing computation into network switches, or rethinking how chips are wired together, they are all trying to close the gap between how fast chips can compute and how fast they can share what they have computed — because until that gap closes, adding more chips buys diminishing returns.
